blocks.content: 1. Problem Statement

blocks.text:
Almost everyone who has worked with code has hit this moment: you have a stack trace, a config file, a log dump, or a snippet of code, and you need to hand it to someone else fast. Screenshots are clumsy, you cannot copy text out of them. Email is slow and formats everything wrong. So instead you paste the raw text into a box on a website, click a button, and get back a short link. You send that link, the other person opens it, and they see exactly what you saw, character for character.

That is the entire job of a pastebin: accept a block of text, store it durably, and hand back a short, shareable link that reproduces that exact text on demand. It sounds almost identical to a URL shortener, and at a glance it is, both systems turn something long into something short and shareable. But the resemblance stops at the front door.

A URL shortener stores a pointer, a few hundred bytes that say "go here instead." A pastebin stores the actual content, sometimes a few lines, sometimes a ten thousand line log dump. A redirect is a stateless, instant operation with nothing to render. A paste means owning the entire read experience: how the text is stored, how long it lives, who is allowed to see it, and what happens the moment it stops being needed. Those differences are what make this an interesting system to design in its own right, not just a reskin of the URL shortener problem.

So before reaching for any diagrams, it is worth being precise about the job. We need a service that accepts a block of text, plus a handful of optional settings (how long it should live, who can see it, what language it is written in), and returns a short link. Visiting that link returns the original text, unmodified, for as long as the paste is supposed to exist, and not a moment longer.

items: Syntax highlighting hints: a user can tag a paste as Python, or JSON, or a raw log file, so the viewer can render it with proper coloring instead of a flat gray wall of text.
Expiration: a paste can be set to expire after a fixed duration, a specific date, or after being read exactly once ("burn after reading"), so sensitive debug output does not sit around forever.

Visibility levels: a paste can be public (discoverable), unlisted (viewable only by anyone who has the link), or private (viewable only by its owner, or explicitly, an authenticated set of collaborators).
Paste management: a signed in user can see every paste they have created and delete the ones they no longer want live.
Raw content access: a plain text endpoint that returns the body with no HTML wrapper at all, useful for piping straight into a terminal with curl.

blocks.content: 2.3 What this system explicitly does not do

blocks.text: It is worth being just as clear about the boundary as about the feature list. This is a text pastebin, not a general file host, arbitrary binary uploads, images, and executables are out of scope. There is also no live collaborative editing, a paste is a write once, read many artifact, not a shared document that multiple people type into at the same time. Both of those are reasonable products, they are just different products with very different consistency and storage requirements.

3. Non-Functional Requirements

blocks.text: Functional requirements describe what the system does, non-functional requirements describe how well it needs to do it. For a pastebin, several of these targets end up genuinely different from a URL shortener's, and it is worth being explicit about why rather than copying numbers across.

3.1 Scalability

blocks.text: The system needs to comfortably absorb millions of new pastes a day and a modest multiple of that in reads. The interesting scaling pressure here is not raw request rate the way it is for a URL shortener, it is the sheer volume of bytes: a paste can be a few lines or a few hundred kilobytes, and the storage layer has to handle that variance gracefully.

3.2 Availability

blocks.text: A broken paste link is annoying, someone shared a debugging session or a snippet and it is suddenly unreachable, but it is rarely as visible or as business critical as a broken marketing redirect. That difference in blast radius is a legitimate reason to target a slightly less aggressive availability number here than a URL shortener would, and still take it seriously.

3.3 Reliability

blocks.text: Once a paste is created, its content must not change and must not disappear before its expiration time, if it has one. Losing a paste's body early, or silently corrupting it, is a correctness bug, not a performance hiccup, and it is exactly the kind of bug that erodes trust in a tool people use to share sensitive debugging context.

3.4 Performance

blocks.text: Reading a paste should feel instant, comfortably under a couple hundred milliseconds even when it involves a real fetch from blob storage. Creating a paste can tolerate a bit more latency than that, since a write happens once and is rarely on a tight interactive loop the way a redirect click is.

3.5 Fault Tolerance and Consistency

blocks.text: When a component is unhealthy, a slow cache node, a struggling shard, the system should degrade gracefully rather than fail outright. A slightly stale view count is a non-issue, nobody is watching it in real time. A paste that silently reappears after its expiration time, on the other hand, is a real problem, especially for anything set to self destruct for privacy reasons.

3.6 Security

blocks.text: A pastebin is a tempting target for abuse: it is an easy place to dump phishing kits, leaked credentials, or malware payloads behind an anonymous, disposable link. Rate limiting, content scanning, and careful handling of visibility are not an afterthought here, they are close to the core of what makes this a defensible design.

"Should pastes expire by default, or live forever unless deleted?" This decides whether a background reaper is a core piece of the system or an optional add on.

blocks.text: 5.1 Why a random id, not a sequential one
blocks.content: 5.1 Why a random id, not a sequential one

blocks.text: This is the first genuinely different decision from the URL shortener playbook, and it is worth dwelling on. A URL shortener can get away with a sequential counter encoded into base62, because the thing a short code points to is never secret, enumerating every code just wastes an attacker's time visiting random destinations. A pastebin is different the moment visibility levels enter the picture: an unlisted paste's entire security model rests on the id itself being effectively unguessable. If ids were sequential, walking the counter would let anyone enumerate every unlisted paste ever created, including ones their owners assumed were private by obscurity.

There is enormous headroom, but unlike a sequential scheme, headroom alone is not proof of safety, since two independent random draws really can collide. §24 works out exactly how often that happens and why it is still a non issue.

6.1 Writes and reads

6.3 Bandwidth

blocks.text: Write bandwidth is trivial: 58 writes a second at 10 KB each is about 580 KB per second. Read bandwidth at 580 reads a second, same average size, is about 5.8 MB per second. Even at peak, 3,000 reads a second times 10 KB tops out around 30 MB per second, well within what a handful of instances push without strain. Bandwidth was never going to be the bottleneck here, storage growth is.

https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785228701695-231765871.png
blocks.alt: The write service stores the body first; if the metadata write fails afterward, the orphaned blob is harmless and expires on its own, while the client simply retries

blocks.text: Order matters more than it looks like it should here. The write service stores the body in the blob store before it writes the metadata row, never the other way around. If the metadata write then fails for any reason, a lock timeout, a network blip, the result is an orphaned blob object with no metadata pointing at it, which is completely harmless, a lifecycle rule quietly expires it later, and the client simply sees an error and retries the whole create. Flip that order, write metadata first, and a failure after that point would leave a metadata row pointing at content that was never actually saved, a broken paste that looks like it exists but returns nothing when opened. One ordering fails safe, the other does not, and that is worth being explicit about in an interview rather than treating storage writes as interchangeable.

Seven days later, the expiration reaper notices this paste's time is up and removes it from the metadata store, the blob store, and the cache, all without anyone having to remember to clean it up manually.

blocks.text: 14.2 Why immutability makes this almost trivial
blocks.content: 14.2 Why immutability makes this almost trivial
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785228662916-529989304.png
blocks.alt: Mutable data forces every write to invalidate the cache; an immutable paste can be cached until its own TTL with no invalidation logic at all

blocks.text: Most systems that cache something mutable have to solve a genuinely hard problem: what happens to the cached copy when the underlying data changes. A paste sidesteps that problem entirely, once created, its content never changes. There is no write that needs to invalidate a cached read, no race between an update and a stale cache hit to worry about. The only way a cached paste ever needs to leave the cache before natural eviction is if it gets deleted or expires, and even that case has a clean answer: set the cache entry's own TTL to match the paste's expiresAt, so the cache entry disappears on its own schedule, in sync with the source of truth, rather than needing an explicit invalidation call from the reaper.

15. Message Queues & Asynchronous Processing

blocks.text: Two jobs in this system are a poor fit for the synchronous request path, and both get handed off to queues instead.

15.1 Abuse scanning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785228664419-699530204.png
blocks.alt: The write service publishes a new paste event to a queue; a scanner service consumes it and flags or takes down malicious content after the fact

blocks.text: Scanning a paste's content for known malicious patterns, phishing kit signatures, leaked credential formats, malware payloads, takes real time, more than a create request should ever have to wait on. So the write service publishes a lightweight event, just the paste id, onto a scan queue the moment a paste is created, and returns to the client immediately. A pool of scanner service consumers drains that queue independently, and a paste that gets flagged is taken down after the fact rather than being blocked before it ever exists. That trade means a small window exists where a bad paste is briefly live, but it keeps the create path fast for the overwhelming majority of legitimate pastes, and §24.3 works through why that trade is worth making.

15.2 Expiration and cleanup
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785228666250-872615566.png
blocks.alt: A TTL index or scheduled scan feeds the reaper, which decrements the blob reference count, deletes the metadata row, and evicts the cache entry

blocks.text: The reaper runs on a schedule, querying the expiresAt index from §10.1 for anything past due, in small batches rather than one giant sweep, so it never holds a long scan against the metadata table. blocks.title: Retries and a dead letter queue
blocks.text: A blob delete or a metadata delete can fail transiently, a network blip, a throttled API call. Failed reaper operations get retried with exponential backoff, and after a small number of attempts, land on a dead letter queue for manual inspection rather than being silently dropped or retried forever. Losing track of a paste that should have expired is a privacy bug, not just an inconvenience, so failures here are treated seriously rather than best effort.

17.1 Horizontal over vertical
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785228673800-361348471.png

blocks.text: A paste that unexpectedly gets shared to a huge audience, posted to a large forum or picked up by a bot, can see its read rate spike by orders of magnitude in minutes. If that paste's cache entry happens to expire during the spike, every one of those simultaneous requests falls through to storage at once, a thundering herd that can overload the database far more than the raw read volume alone would suggest. Request coalescing, where the first miss for a given id triggers the storage fetch and every concurrent request for that same id waits on that one in-flight fetch rather than starting its own, is the standard defense, and it is worth naming explicitly as the mitigation for this scenario in an interview.

blocks.text: It is worth working out exactly how rare that collision retry actually is, since "rare" alone is not a convincing argument. https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785228690258-966959727.png
blocks.alt: Storing the body in a database row bloats the buffer cache and backups, while a blob store keeps it cheap and independently scalable

blocks.text: Storing the raw text directly in a column on the metadata row would be simpler to build on day one, one write, one table. It falls apart at scale for reasons covered in §7.7: large row values inflate the database's buffer cache with data that is never actually queried by content, bloat every backup and replication stream, and tie the cost and scaling curve of cheap, bulky text storage to the cost and scaling curve of a database built for fast structured lookups. Splitting the two, as this design does, lets each piece scale on its own economics.

It falls apart at scale for reasons covered in §7.7: large row values inflate the database's buffer cache with data that is never actually queried by content, bloat every backup and replication stream, and tie the cost and scaling curve of cheap, bulky text storage to the cost and scaling curve of a database built for fast structured lookups. Splitting the two, as this design does, lets each piece scale on its own economics.
24.3 Synchronous vs asynchronous abuse scanning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785228691743-492072039.png
blocks.alt: Scanning synchronously makes every create pay the latency cost, while async scanning keeps creates fast and takes down flagged content after the fact

blocks.text: Scanning every paste before confirming its creation would catch malicious content before it is ever reachable, at the cost of making every single create request, including the overwhelming majority that are completely legitimate, pay for a scan that usually finds nothing. Scanning asynchronously keeps the create path fast for everyone and accepts a short window where a bad paste could theoretically be live before takedown. Given how the vast majority of pastebin abuse is discovered and reported over a longer timescale than that brief window anyway, this design accepts that trade in favor of not punishing every legitimate user's create latency for the sake of the rare malicious one.

items: A paste right at the size cap: a 1 MB paste should stream to the blob store rather than being buffered entirely in application memory, so a burst of maximum-size creates cannot exhaust a service instance's memory.
A paste going viral mid-life: covered in §23.2, request coalescing prevents a cache expiry from turning into a thundering herd.

Clock skew across regions affecting TTL: if one region's clock drifts ahead, it could expire a paste slightly before another region does. Using a single, centrally assigned expiresAt timestamp computed at creation time, rather than having each region compute its own countdown independently, keeps expiration consistent regardless of any single region's local clock drift.
A shared blob reference during expiry: the reference counting from §11.3 exists specifically so reaping one paste's expired row never deletes content another, still-active paste still depends on.

An unlisted link forwarded somewhere unintended: this is a real risk with the unlisted visibility tier, and it is an inherent trade of that model, not a bug. Anything genuinely sensitive belongs in the private tier, which enforces ownership rather than relying on the link staying secret.

Burn-after-read racing two simultaneous opens: if two requests for the same burn-after-read paste arrive at nearly the same instant, the read service's mark-as-expired step needs to be atomic, so exactly one of the two requests successfully reads the content and the other sees it as already gone, rather than both succeeding.

items: "What stops someone from writing a script that creates a million pastes a minute?" The rate limiter from §21 and the Complete Code Implementation section, plus a hard per-paste size cap, are the first line of defense.

"How would you support a paste with a hundred million views?" That is exactly the cache stampede scenario from §23.2, request coalescing plus a sufficiently long cache TTL for hot content handles it without every read touching storage.

"What happens if the scanner falls behind?" The scan queue depth metric from §22 pages someone, and the scanner service auto-scales on that same signal per §17.2, before a meaningful amount of unscanned content accumulates.

"Could you make paste ids shorter?" Only by giving up either the random id space needed for unguessability, discussed in §5.1, or by accepting a meaningfully higher collision rate than the one worked out in §24.1, there is a real trade there, not a free lunch.

"How is this different from designing a URL shortener?" The redirect target in a URL shortener is a pointer to someone else's content and is never secret; a paste's body is the actual content, self-hosted, filterable for abuse, and in some visibility tiers, genuinely intended to stay confidential, which changes the storage, caching, and security model throughout.

from datetime import datetime


class PasteMetadataService:
    def __init__(self, id_generator, blob_store, paste_repository, scan_queue_publisher):
        self.id_generator = id_generator
        self.blob_store = blob_store
        self.paste_repository = paste_repository
        self.scan_queue_publisher = scan_queue_publisher

    def create(self, request):
        # Store the body first, an orphaned blob on a later failure is
        # harmless, an orphaned metadata row pointing at nothing is not.
        content_hash = self.blob_store.store(request.body)

        paste = Paste(
            paste_id=self.id_generator.generate(),
            owner_id=request.owner_id,
            visibility=request.visibility,
            language_hint=request.language_hint,
            content_hash=content_hash,
            size_bytes=len(request.body),
            created_at=datetime.utcnow(),
            expires_at=request.expires_at,
            burn_after_read=request.burn_after_read,
        )

        self.paste_repository.save(paste)
        # Off the hot path: a flagged paste gets pulled down after the
        # fact instead of blocking every legitimate create request.
        self.scan_queue_publisher.publish(paste.paste_id)
        return paste

from datetime import datetime

BATCH_SIZE = 500


class PasteExpirationReaper:
    def __init__(self, paste_repository, blob_store, cache):
        self.paste_repository = paste_repository
        self.blob_store = blob_store
        self.cache = cache

    def sweep(self):
        # Runs on a schedule, small batches so a slow sweep never holds
        # a long-lived scan against the metadata table.
        expired = self.paste_repository.find_expired_batch(datetime.utcnow(), BATCH_SIZE)
        for paste in expired:
            # Only drops the object once its reference count hits zero.
            self.blob_store.release(paste.content_hash)
            self.paste_repository.delete(paste.paste_id)
            self.cache.evict(paste.paste_id)

import threading
import time

MAX_TOKENS = 20
REFILL_PER_SECOND = 0.5  # one new paste every 2 seconds, sustained


class _Bucket:
    def __init__(self, tokens, last_refill):
        self.tokens = tokens
        self.last_refill = last_refill
        self.lock = threading.Lock()


class PasteRateLimiter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.buckets = {}
        self.buckets_lock = threading.Lock()

    def try_acquire(self, key: str) -> bool:
        # Called once per create request, keyed by user id or IP for
        # anonymous callers.
        with self.buckets_lock:
            bucket = self.buckets.setdefault(key, _Bucket(MAX_TOKENS, time.monotonic()))

        with bucket.lock:
            self._refill(bucket)
            if bucket.tokens >= 1.0:
                bucket.tokens -= 1.0
                return True
            return False

    def _refill(self, bucket):
        now = time.monotonic()
        elapsed = now - bucket.last_refill
        bucket.tokens = min(MAX_TOKENS, bucket.tokens + elapsed * REFILL_PER_SECOND)
        bucket.last_refill = now

blocks.title: Sizing the refill rate
blocks.text: A refill rate of 0.5 tokens a second with a 20 token bucket allows a legitimate burst, someone pasting several files in quick succession, while still capping sustained abuse at one paste every two seconds per key, far below what any real automated attack would find useful.
